content: If drug susceptibility testing (DST) were conducted as a secondary step, the target population for such testing would consist of individuals with bacteriologically confirmed tuberculosis (TB), estimated to be approximately 7 million people globally. However, the market for a test to detect bedaquiline (BDQ) resistance is distinct, as the current performance characteristics of molecular tests for BDQ resistance remain uncertain. Additionally, BDQ is currently recommended only for use in patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB). Consequently, a test for BDQ resistance would only be applicable as a follow-up test if rifampin resistance has already been confirmed, given that a higher prevalence of resistance increases the positive predictive value (PPV) for detecting resistance to a specific anti-TB agent. Minimal training requirements for such tests would involve healthcare workers with limited or no laboratory skills (beginner users), while moderate training would involve healthcare workers with basic to moderate laboratory competency (competent or proficient users). Implementation of these tests at peripheral healthcare levels should be feasible, leveraging existing infrastructure such as smear microscopy facilities. However, these tests could also be deployed at higher levels of care. Ideally, testing for resistance to second-line anti-TB agents should be integrated into the same specimen analysis, although separate reactions may be required. The prioritization of anti-TB agents for testing includes rifampin (RIF), isoniazid (INH), fluoroquinolones (FQs, including levofloxacin and moxifloxacin), and BDQ. Additional drugs such as pyrazinamide (PZA), linezolid (LZD), pretomanid (Pa), delamanid (DLM), clofazimine (CFZ), amikacin (AMK), and d-cycloserine (DCS) are considered in descending order of importance. This prioritization aligns with the End TB Strategy, which emphasizes universal access to DST and the necessity of susceptibility testing to ensure effective TB treatment, particularly for drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). Resistance to FQs is critical for both first-line and second-line regimens and is central to the updated definitions of pre-extensively drug-resistant TB (pre-XDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB). BDQ, now a Group A medicine, is included in all DR-TB regimens, including shorter MDR/RR-TB regimens. New tests should guide decision-making for shorter and novel MDR/RR-TB treatment regimens. The molecular basis of BDQ resistance is not yet fully understood, but this is expected to improve in the coming years. The addition of BDQ-resistance detection to tests may require new technologies, and an indicative price for such tests cannot currently be determined. Similarly, the cost of assays for newer drugs like DLM, LZD, and CFZ remains unpredictable. Phenotypic DST for first-line and second-line drugs is estimated to cost between $50 and $100, and new tests should ideally be priced lower, based on evidence of production costs and reasonable profit margins. Cost-effectiveness analysis is essential to justify pricing and ensure access, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The price of a single Xpert XDR-TB assay, which includes testing for INH, FQs, second-line injectables, and ethionamide, is approximately $20. Expanding such tests to all TB patients or presumptive TB cases would significantly increase the market. Rapid turnaround time for test results is critical to reducing pretreatment loss to follow-up. Ideally, all technologies should produce results within six hours, aligning with typical workday durations in peripheral settings. Delays in DST can lead to inappropriate treatment and ongoing disease transmission. Tests should be designed to minimize sample processing steps and should not require additional samples for follow-up reactions. The daily throughput of tests should meet the needs of peripheral centers, which typically require fewer than 10 tests per day. Operational characteristics of the tests should include compatibility with sputum and other clinically relevant specimens, such as gastric aspirates, induced sputum, nasopharyngeal aspirates, stool, and extrapulmonary TB samples. Minimal biosafety infrastructure should be required, as biosafety cabinets are unlikely to be available in peripheral settings. The technology must pose a low safety risk to healthcare workers, comparable to smear microscopy. Waste disposal requirements should align with those for smear microscopy to avoid increasing the burden of infectious waste. Finally, the test should be adaptable to evolving needs, including the ability to incorporate new drugs and adjust sequence interpretation for sequencing-based assays. Multiplex testing or the ability to perform different tests on the same platform will likely increase the acceptability of new assays.
